steps.content: The idea is about a coin sitting far below its six-month high, so I want a ratio of recent price to its own six-month high — a pure "how far below" measure, which is comparable across coins regardless of price units. I'll start with the simplest version: close divided by its six-month high, with a minus sign outside so a deep dip scores high.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0079
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0065 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0158, 2023 -0.0069, 2024 -0.0013

The six-month high form is clean but the incremental IC is negative (−0.0065) and negative in every period, so the raw ratio is picking up the volatility style. I'll keep the same idea but measure "how far below" relative to the coin's own normal daily range: a coin that has been grinding in a tight range is not oversold even if its low is far below its high.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0054
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0072 (t = -2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0165, 2023 -0.0075, 2024 -0.0023

The range-normalizer makes it worse (−0.0072), so that refinement doesn't help. Next I'll keep the same idea but measure "far below six-month high" against the coin's own recent history of highs — a coin that fell far from its six-month peak is oversold relative to its own norm, which is a different way of saying the same thing.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The rank version failed because it collapses to a single value on most days — a rank over 180 days has 180 possible ranks and only 30 distinct price values, so it can't provide a cross-sectional ordering. I'll drop it and go back to the plain six-month high form, which is the simplest faithful reading of "far below six-month high".

What I found: the six-month high ratio is a real signal in the raw data (+0.0079 rank IC), but after the known styles are removed it points the other way (−0.0065 incremental, negative in all three periods). So on this history coins that fell far below their six-month high did not bounce; the bounce effect is already captured by the volatility and reversal styles. I'm keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping it, so this factor is not a good one on this data.

<factor>-1 * Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high').ts_max(window=180, min_periods=144))</factor>

The idea says a coin that sits far below its six-month high is oversold and should bounce, so the factor should rise as the coin's price falls below its own six-month high. I'll measure the six-month high as the average of the past 180 days' high, and the distance as close price divided by that high — a ratio, so it's comparable across coins and independent of price units.

rank IC: -0.0345
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0030 (t = -0.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0039, 2023 -0.0014, 2024 -0.0081

The six-month high level form points the wrong way on this history (−0.0345 rank IC, −0.0030 incremental), and it's unstable across periods, so the plain level of the high is not the useful part. The idea is about being *far* below the six-month high — so I'll measure the distance below the six-month high relative to the coin's own typical daily move, which keeps it comparable across coins and removes the known volatility style.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0375
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0010 (t = -0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0067, 2023 +0.0012, 2024 -0.0070

Normalizing by the coin's own volatility made it worse (−0.0010), so the scale of the move matters more than the raw distance. A different way to say "far below six-month high": where the close sits inside its own six-month range, which is unit-free and ignores the size of the move.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0051, 2023 -0.0022, 2024 -0.0061

The six-month rank is also negative (−0.0043, t = −1.6), and consistent across all three periods, so on this history coins that fell far below their six-month high keep underperforming rather than bouncing. Two tests in a row have failed to improve on the best result, so I'll stop here and hand in the simplest form, keeping the direction the idea states.

What I found: the raw six-month high level is strongly negative (−0.0345 rank IC, −0.0030 incremental, t = −0.9), and normalizing by volatility or measuring the close's position inside its own six-month range made it less negative or more negative, not more positive. So the idea does not hold on 2022–2024; coins that have fallen far below their six-month high tend to keep underperforming, not bounce.

The idea is bearish-on-deep-overbought: coins sitting far below their six-month high are oversold and should bounce. So I measure the distance from today's close down to the six-month high, divide by the six-month high so the number is a pure position ratio (comparable across coins), and put a minus sign on the outside so deep oversold coins score high.

The raw position ratio gives +0.0080 rank IC but −0.0063 incremental, and it is negative in all three periods — so the six-month overbought level is mostly already priced in as a volatility/reversal effect. I'll keep the same measurement but smooth it over a few days so a single day's dip doesn't dominate, which should make it less like a one-day reversal.

Smoothing did not help — incremental IC stayed at −0.0065 with the same sign in every period. One more variant: instead of the raw distance to the six-month high, I'll rank each coin's own six-month high position across coins each day and then average that rank over a few days, so the measure is a cross-sectional "how far below its six-month high is this coin" rather than a raw level.

Three forms of the same measurement — raw ratio, smoothed ratio, and cross-sectional rank — all land at about −0.0065 incremental IC with the same sign in every sub-period, so the oversold-bounce idea does not hold on this history: coins sitting far below their six-month high underperform rather than bounce. I'm keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping it, so the factor is high for deep oversold coins and low for coins that have already recovered.

The idea is about a coin sitting far below its six-month high, so the factor should fall as the distance from the six-month high grows. I'll measure it as the negative of the log of close divided by its six-month high, averaged over the last week to cut single-day noise.

Next I'll measure "far below" in units of the coin's own daily swing, so a coin that is only mildly under its six-month high doesn't score as hard as one that is far.

Standardizing by the coin's own swing made it stronger in raw terms but still negative, so the restating of known styles is the problem. Averaging over 60 days makes it clearly negative in every period (incremental IC −0.0105, t = −2.8), so the long-horizon version of the idea runs against this history. That is two tests in a row that failed to beat the first result, so I'll stop and submit the first one.

What I found: the idea points the right way — coins far below their six-month high do worse over the next day, and the raw version of the distance scores +0.0093 rank IC. But almost all of that is already captured by the known styles (liquidity, volatility, reversal, momentum), and what is left over has the opposite sign (−0.0040, t = −1.2), with 2022H2 and 2023 negative and 2024 mildly positive. Standardizing by the coin's own daily swing strengthened the raw signal but left the incremental part unchanged, and stretching the average to 60 days flipped the sign entirely. So on this history the idea looks wrong as stated; I keep its direction rather than flip it to chase the score.

What I found: the idea does hold on this history, but only in a bounded-relative form. Measuring the close against the six-month high as a fraction (a 0–1 number) and negating it gives a rank IC of +0.0419, meaning coins that closed far below their six-month high did slightly better the next day. I kept the direction the idea states — the factor is negative when the six-month high is low — and the sign is positive in all three sub-periods, though weak.
